title: The Hungry Cellar
premise: Ada Quintana returns to the family farmhouse to settle her twin sister Marisol's estate, only to find her childhood imaginary friend, Wren, waiting on the porch—unchanged after thirty years. As Ada catalogs the house for sale, she learns Marisol spent her life feeding something in the cellar a bargain their grandmother struck: one Quintana stays, always, and the family's luck holds. Ada, the skeptic who left and thrived while Marisol stayed and withered, must decide whether love for her dead sister means honoring the duty or breaking it—and discovers that 'Wren' is the cellar itself, hungry for a believer. In the end, Ada signs nothing, burns the papers at sunrise, and walks away whole—but leaves the door unlocked, because belonging, she finally understands, was never about staying.
about_author: Ada Whitlock grew up on a failing orchard farm in upstate New York, where she was told never to go into the root cellar after dark. She writes horror about families who mistake inheritance for love.

chapters.title: The Wrong Twin
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She arrives at the farmhouse to bury Marisol, resentful of being the sibling who lived. At the funeral, relatives avoid her eyes and someone whispers that the wrong one died. Emotional beat: guilt sharpened into defensiveness.

chapters.title: Porch Light
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. On her first night back, she finds Wren—a small figure from her childhood imaginings—sitting on the porch steps, exactly as she drew him at age seven. He says only, 'You came back.' Beat: uncanny dread wrapped in nostalgia.

chapters.title: Inventory
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She begins cataloging the house for the estate lawyer, finding rooms frozen mid-life: Marisol's calendar marked with feeding schedules, jars of offerings, ledgers going back generations. Beat: the skeptic's rational explanations start costing effort.

chapters.title: The Ledgers
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The ledgers record payments made by every Quintana woman since 1890: flour, blood, years of life. Marisol's final entry reads 'balance due: one.' Beat: horror as bookkeeping; duty revealed as debt.

chapters.title: What Wren Wants
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Ada and Wren, who speaks in fragments. Wren insists he protected them, that he kept the bad thing fed so it never took a child. Beat: tenderness toward something that may be lying.

chapters.title: Neighbor's Warning
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Elderly neighbor Ruth Delgado, who knew the grandmother, tells her the cellar predates the house—the Quintanas built around it, not over it. Beat: the family didn't invite the hunger; they inherited it.

chapters.title: Marisol's Room
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She finally enters her sister's bedroom and finds drawings identical to her own childhood sketches—both twins drew Wren, but only Ada stopped believing. Beat: grief reframed as abandonment; Marisol believed alone.

chapters.title: The Cellar Door
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Against every instinct she opens the cellar and descends. It is warm, breathing, lined with names scratched into stone—every Quintana woman, including Marisol's, freshly cut. Beat: visceral terror and terrible intimacy.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Lawyer POV. The estate reading reveals an addendum in the will: whoever signs the transfer papers becomes 'resident' by law and by older law. The signing is set for Friday. Beat: bureaucratic horror; the trap has paperwork.

chapters.title: Wren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Wren POV. He offers Ada a deal: sign nothing, stay seven nights, and he'll show her what really happened to Marisol. Beat: seduction of answers; the reader doubts him more than Ada does.

chapters.title: First Night
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Night one: the house rearranges itself around memories, doors leading to 1994. Ada relives the day she promised Marisol she'd come back and didn't for twenty years. Beat: shame as haunting.

chapters.title: The Bad Thing Below
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Something else lives under the cellar floor—older than Wren, hungrier. Wren isn't the monster; he's the lock. Beat: reversal that recontextualizes every prior scare.

chapters.title: Ruth's Story
chapters.summary: Ruth POV. Ruth confesses her own family once held a similar bargain and broke it; her brother was taken in a single night, politely, without a sound. Beat: cost of disbelief established through witness.

chapters.title: Feeding Schedule
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She follows Marisol's last week via receipts and phone records: her sister spent her final days preparing the house for Ada's arrival—stocking food, mending the porch light, leaving the ledgers open. Beat: devastating realization that Marisol's death was a handoff.

chapters.title: Night Four: The Offer
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The Bad Thing speaks through the house itself, offering Ada everything Marisol ever wanted if she just believes. Ada nearly does. Beat: temptation at its peak; skepticism revealed as armor, not strength.

chapters.title: What Marisol Knew
chapters.summary: Wren POV. Wren shows Ada the truth: Marisol didn't die of illness—she gave herself as the year's payment early, buying Ada time to arrive before Friday's signing. Beat: love against duty crystallized; guilt becomes purpose.

chapters.title: Breaking the Ledger
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She tries to destroy the ledgers and sever the debt. The house fights back—walls weep, the stairs lengthen, Wren screams that unbelief won't save her, only a new covenant will. Beat: climax approach; force fails where understanding hasn't been tried.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Friday. Lawyer POV and Ada's POV interleave as the signing begins. The pen won't write anything but Ada's name. Ruth arrives with the Delgado family Bible and a forgotten clause: debts can be transferred by forgiveness, not signature. Beat: climax; the weapon is grace, not defiance.

chapters.title: Believing Is Not Obeying
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She chooses to believe—in Wren, in Marisol, in the family—without signing. Belief freely given starves the contract; the Bad Thing loses its claim because no one was tricked. Beat: thematic resolution; love without obligation breaks the cycle.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She burns the papers at dawn as the cellar goes cold and quiet. Wren begins to fade, thanking her—not for saving him, but for coming back. Beat: bittersweet farewell to childhood itself.

chapters.title: Estate Closed
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. She buries Marisol properly, donates the house to a land trust with covenants no one will read closely, and keeps one ledger page as memory. Beat: quiet aftermath; inheritance redefined as story rather than debt.

chapters.title: Unlocked
chapters.summary: Final image, Ada's POV. Driving away, she looks back: the porch light is on, the front door standing open, and on the step, a child's drawing of two sisters. She doesn't stop. Beat: belonging carried forward; the door stays open for whatever comes next.
